label: header
text: THE CHINA MAIL:

label: paragraph_title
text: AID FOR COAL INDUSTRY.

label: paragraph_title
text: GOVERNMENT SUBSIDY OF TEN MILLIONS.

label: text
text: Another Thrust

label: text
text: In the House of Commons yesterday the Prime Minister's motion for a subsidy of £10,000,000 to the coal mining industry was carried after a spirited debate, in the course of which foreign agitators and the Communist elements in the Trade Unions were strongly denounced.

label: text
text: Agitators

label: text
text: The House of Commons was crowded and animated when Mr. S. Baldwin (Prime Minister) moved the Supplementary Estimate of £10,000,000 for a "subvention to aid wages in the coal mining industry," amid labour cries of "no; profits."

label: text
text: Mr. Baldwin said that there was no means of avoiding a strike without temporary Government help. He was still convinced that the Government took a right and wise course. He had been called a coward. "Well, it was much easier to be rattled into a fight than rattled into peace," (Cheers). We were confronted with a great alliance of Trade Unionists who had the power and will (Labour cheers) to indict enormous and irreparable damage to the country. (Ministerial cheers).

label: paragraph_title
text: POLICY OF FORCE.

label: text
text: Mr. Baldwin, amid Labourite cries of dissent and Ministerial cheers, said that there was apparently a deliberate and avowed policy of force and stoppage regardless of suffering. He was not aware if that policy was endorsed by the whole of the Labour Party. If that was so he did not see how a constitutional Government could live. He had secured at a price, an immensely valuable respite. He had done his utmost in the last year or two to secure industrial peace, but if we were again confronted with such a challenge "let me just say that no minority in a free country ever yet coerced a whole community." (Cheers: Labourite Cries of "The Coal owners.") "I am convinced that if time comes when the community must protect itself with the full strength of the Government behind it, the community will do so, and the response of the community will astonish the forces of anarchy the world over." (Ministerial cheers: and angry Labour cries.) "I say this merely as a warning and I know I am stating the deep, fundamental, and widespread belief of the vast majority of the great free people of this country."

label: text
text: Mr. Ramsay MacDonald regretted deeply Mr. Baldwin's closing sentences. He declared that anarchy never occurred in any State unless conditioned by a feeble and reactionary Government. He asserted that public opinion was united to a most extraordinary degree against the coal miners for posting notices. The Trade Union's had to prepare their own defence, and their extraordinary manifestation of industrial will was amply justified. Mr. MacDonald admitted that the situation last Thursday could only be met by a subsidy, though he rejected a subsidy in principle. He believed that the inquiry would find that national control of the mines was essential.

label: paragraph_title
text: DRIVEN BY THREATS.

label: text
text: Mr. D. Lloyd George, who was subjected to many interruptions and fronical laughter from the back Labour benches, declared the bargain to be practically nationalisation, with a Government guarantee, but without control. Mr. Baldwin had been driven to that by threats of direct actionists. Democracy was doomed if it surrendered to the compulsion of the minority.

label: text
text: Mr. Robert Smillie (Labour), referring to conditions in countries with which British coal competed, said that there was money invested in coal mines in India in which the conditions were similar to those existing in Britain a century ago, and there would be revolution in Britain if miners were forced down to such a position.

label: paragraph_title
text: CONSERVATIVES ALARMED

label: text
text: Sir R. Horne was of opinion that the subsidy could not meet the difficulties which arose from the condition of the industries of the world which the Government could not control. If people were led to believe that they could live upon subsidies, the plight next May would be worse than today

label: text
text: Mr. W. Gretton (Conservative) declared that Conservatives were alarmed at the surrender to force. The Government's action would strengthen the position of the communists and extremists within the Trade Union. He hoped that the Government would give an assurance that the policy would not be one of subsidies.

label: text
text: Mr. J. R. Clynes (Labour) said that the Premier's speech unwarrantably cast aspersions on the workers, who had their backs against the well. The miners would have been craven cowards if they had not resisted these wage reductions, and the rest of the workers would not have been worthy of the name of comrades if they had not stood behind them. (Labour cheers).

label: paragraph_title
text: A BREATHING SPACE.

label: text
text:
Mr. Winston Churchill (Chancellor of the Exchequer), replying to the debate, said that it was agreed that the settlement was not final but a breathing space, secured in the hope that the community would be spared a conflict.
'This' subsidy might amount to

label: text
text: the sacrifice of money not made without achieving an effective advantage. Nobody liked a subsidy, but fewer would have liked a general stoppage.

label: text
text: The Government's decision therefore was best in the interests of the public. He had not provided for a subsidy in the Budget, but did not intend to propose any new taxation. The matter could be considered when the next Budget was framed. The miners' wages had not been raised above the pre-war figure to the extent of other less dangerous occupations. The Government declined to discern in the miners' resistance any wish to challenge the State. (Labour' cheers). There was a challenge from the forces deliberately working to promote discontent. It would be a great mistake to identify the masses of their fellow countrymen with those forces which were inspired by foreign propaganda. (Cheers).

label: text
text: Parliament must also be protected from the threat of the Trade Unions, and it must not be supposed that because the Government worked for peace it was incapable of defending a great institution. (Cheers).

label: paragraph_title
text: VOTE CARRIED.

label: text
text: A section of the Liberals challenged a division on the Supplementary Estimate, which was adopted by 351 votes to 16.

label: paragraph_title
text: LOCAL WEDDING.

label: paragraph_title
text: YESTERDÁY'S PRETTY EVENT.

label: paragraph_title
text: CAPT. BLOXHAM MARRIED.

label: text
text: St. John's Cathedral was the scene of a pretty wedding yesterday afternoon, the parties being Capt. H. F. Bloxham, Superintendent of Victoria Gaol, and Miss Audrey Jones.

label: text
text: Captain Bloxham is the son of the late Mr. Fitzherbert Bloxham of Andover Herts, and the bride is the only daughter of the late Mr. Robert and Mrs. Jones of Manchester.

label: text
text: The bride wore a simple short sleeved gown of white georgette, trimmed with silver beads and pearls, with a silver train, veil and wreath and entered the Cathedral on the arm of Mr. D. Burlingham, Assistant Superintendent of Police, who gave her away. Her bouquet was of lilies and Honolulu creeper.

label: text
text: A full choir, singing a hymn, also the Rev. T. B. Powell who officiated at the service, preceded the bride up the aisle. Her attendant was Miss Jackie Scott, who in blue organdie and with a basket of pink rosebuds, made a charming bridesmaid.

label: text
text: Mr. L. H. V. Booth, Assistant Superintendent of Police, was best man.

label: text
text: At the conclusion of the ceremony the bridal pair passed out of the Cathedral under an arch of swords, upheld by European and Indian members of Capt. Bloxham's staff.

label: text
text: Among those subsequently attending at the residence of Capt. Bloxham to toast the health and happiness of the bride and bridegroom were Sir Claud Severn, Mr. A. G. M. Fletcher, Capt. Neville, Lieut.-Comdr. Conway Hake, Mrs. and Miss Holyonk, Mr. C. D. Melbourne and a number of well-known personages.

label: text
text: Capt. and Mrs. Bloxham will spend the honeymoon in Shanghai, leaving to-day by the Empress of Australia.

label: paragraph_title
text: FLOOD SEQUEL.

label: paragraph_title
text: STRICTURES BY THE

label: paragraph_title
text: SYSTEM CRITIÇISED.

label: text
text: The inquiry into the circumstances attending the death of a coolie, who was guarding a steam roller, through the collapse of a retaining wall at the corner of Happy Valley during the recent flood, came to a close yesterday before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry, sitting as Coroner, and a jury composed of Messrs. D. Templeton (foreman), C. J. Joseph and D. O. Russell.

label: paragraph_title
text: The Verdict.

label: text
text: After a lengthy summing up by the Coroner, in which he explained to the jury their duty under the law, the jury retired and brought in the following verdict:—

label: text
text: We find that deceased, Kwong Fat, met his death by misadventure from bodily injuries in accordance with medical evidence submitted. In view of the fact that the Coroner's summing up very ably covers the whole question, which, we as jurors have been called upon to decide, we wish to state that we entirely agree with the same, but would desire to add the following riders:—

label: text
text: The Public Health and Buildings Ordinance in so far as it covers the development of sites and construction of retaining walls needs immediate amendment. Such amendments as regards retaining walls must enforce the drawing up of a proper and complete set of specifications of materials to accompany each submitted plan and farther that not only should each retaining wall be judged individually upon its own merits, but that the final authorisation for construction should rest solely in the hands of the Director of Public Works.

label: text
text: There should be more coordination and co-operation between the Building Authority, the Drainage Engineer and the Executive Engineer in charge of Roads than appears to exist at present.

label: text
text: 3. Regarding development of sites and for the prevention of land slides during such development, we are of the opinion the question of drainage is most vital and in consequence each such development plan must be submitted to the Drainage Engineer for his approval before work is started and that responsibility for such approved drainage during development shall rest solely with the architect in charge.

label: text
text: 4. The architects deserve "ensure" for the attitude adopted by them in regard to their responsibilities.

label: text
text: 5. That the P.W.D. overseer in charge deserves censure for failing to report to his senior officer such a glaring case of inferior workmanship.

label: text
text: We consider that work on the rebuilding of the retaining wall should cease until the Hon. the D.P.W. is himself assured that proper drainage and other precautions have been taken to prevent a repetition of this disastrous occurrence.

label: paragraph_title
text: GONE HOME.

label: paragraph_title
text: KWANGSI GENERAL'S NEW POST.

label: paragraph_title
text: LAU TSUN-WAN DEPARTS.

label: text
text: General Lau Tsun-wan, formerly commander-in-chief of the Kwangsi army in Canton, has left for Indo-China with his staff.

label: text
text: It will be recalled that, together with the Yunnanese, General Lau's troops were defeated by the Kuomintang Cantonese and allies about two months ago. His following has scattered, and it is believed that he is returning to his native province of Kwangsi to enlist new men. At present it is impossible for him to reach Kwangsi except by way of Indo-China.

label: text
text: General Lau may also interview Tuchun Tang Chi-yao, the Yunnan warlord who has led an expedition into Kwangsi. General Lau has been "nominated" by Tuchun Tang as Civil Governor of Kwangsi, this post being at present held by Lai Ting-kaam until General Lau's arrival on the spot. Lai is reported to have recruited over a thousand men for the General's new army.

label: paragraph_title
text: STREET LECTURES.

label: paragraph_title
text: ALLEGED STION THROWING INCIDENT.

label: text
text: There were a large number of witnesses in the case in which two Chinese were charged before Mr. H. A. D. Forrest at- the Central Magistracy yesterday for disorderly conduct and intimidation.

label: text
text: The first accused, Sum Chôi, an accountant at the Kwong Sang Company, was defended by Mr. C. A. S. Russ. Mr. O. H. Lyson appeared for the other accused, Wong Chuen. Mr. T. H. King (Director of Criminal Intelligence) prosecuted.

label: text
text: Amongst those who gave evidence was the complainant, Kong Kitting, who stated that he was appointed by the Trade Maintenance Association to give anti-strike lectures. While he was lecturing in Hillier Street on July 28, he was hit several times by small stones. The next evening the same thing happened, but detectives were mixed up in the crowd on this occasion as he had reported the incident to the Association. Witness could not see the persons who threw the stones.

label: text
text: After several witnesses had given evidence for the defence of Sam Choi, Mr. Russ asked for the acquittal of his client, as he argued that it was a cause of mistaken identity.

label: text
text: His Worship decided to hear the evidence against the second accused before delivering judgment, and adjourned both cases until this afternoon.
